# Ipe: writing scripts and ipelets (complete documentation)

> Ipe is an extensible drawing editor with a Lua scripting interface. This documentation explains how to write Ipe scripts and ipelets (extensions of the editor) in Lua, with complete examples and a reference for all Lua functions.

(Ipe 7.3.1, generated 2026-10-26 from commit 29e6c6c24eca)

## Introduction

Ipe is an extensible drawing editor.  Most of Ipe is written in Lua, and you
can extend it with **ipelets** (Lua files that add functions to the editor's
Ipelets menu), or process Ipe documents from the command line with **scripts**
(run with `ipescript`).  Both use the same Lua library, the table `ipe`.

### Read this first

These are the facts that most often go wrong when writing Ipe scripts and
ipelets.

1. **Script or ipelet?**  A script is run with `ipescript name args` and owns
   the document: it loads it with `ipe.Document(filename)` and saves it with
   `doc:save(filename)`.  An ipelet runs inside the Ipe editor and works on the
   document being edited, through the `model` argument of its `run` function.
2. **An ipelet must never modify the document directly.**  It changes the
   document only through an *undo item* passed to `model:register(t)`, or
   through `model:creation`, `model:transformation`, and `model:setAttribute`,
   which do this for you.  The usual pattern is: clone the page twice
   (`original`, `final`), modify `final`, and register an undo item with
   `undo = _G.revertOriginal` and `redo = _G.revertFinal`.  A script, on
   the other hand, modifies the document directly.
3. **An ipelet defines the global variables** `label` (menu text), `about`,
   and `run` (or `methods`, a table of `{ label=..., run=... }`).  `run`
   is called as `run(model, method_number)`.
4. **An ipelet runs in a restricted environment**: only `_G`, `ipe`, `ipeui`,
   `math`, `string`, `table`, `assert`, `ipairs`, `pairs`, `print`,
   `tonumber`, `tostring`, `prefs`, `config`, `shortcuts`, and `mouse` exist.
   Everything else must be reached through `_G`, for instance `_G.type(x)`,
   `_G.pcall`, `_G.io`.  Writing `type(x)` fails.
5. **Conventions**: pages, views, and objects are numbered from 1; layers are
   identified by name.  Coordinates are in points, the origin is at the
   lower left, and the y-axis points up.  `ipe.Vector`, `ipe.Matrix`, and the
   other geometric classes are immutable values (only `ipe.Rect` is mutable).
   Objects obtained from a page are the page's own objects, not copies: use
   `obj:clone()` and `page:clone()` to copy them.
6. **Errors**: functions that read files return `nil` and an error message;
   calling a function with illegal arguments raises a Lua error.
7. **Dialogs** use `ipeui.Dialog` and can only be shown inside an ipelet (or
   program) that runs inside the Ipe editor.
8. **Test ipelets without the editor** with
   `ipescript run-ipelet myipelet.lua input.ipe output.ipe [name=value ...]`.
   It runs the ipelet on a document with the real model of the Ipe editor,
   accepts dialogs with their default values (or the values given as
   `name=value`), then undoes and redoes the changes and reports if the page
   is not restored exactly.  Use `--select none|all|1,3`, `--method N`,
   `--page N`, `--view N` to control the run.  Always test ipelets this way
   before presenting them as working.
9. **Look at working examples**: the examples in this documentation, and the
   scripts (`scripts/` folder) and ipelets (`ipelets/` folder) that come with
   Ipe.

### How this documentation is organized

* **Guide**: a tutorial on writing scripts and ipelets, with complete
  examples.
* **Lua API reference**: every function of the Lua bindings (geometry,
  objects, attributes, pages, documents, stylesheets), the Ipe editor
  (`AppUi`), dialogs and menus, and the ipelet `model`.

## Scripts and ipelets

Most of the Ipe program is written in the scripting language [Lua](https://www.lua.org), and the same Lua library that Ipe uses to
read, write, and modify documents is available for your own programs.
There are two ways to use it:

* An **Ipe script** is a Lua program that you run from the command
  line using `ipescript`.  A script reads an Ipe document,
  does something with it, and typically writes a new document or prints
  some information.  Scripts are good for batch processing and for
  tasks that you want to run on many files.

* An **ipelet** is an extension of the Ipe editor.  It is a Lua file
  that adds one or more entries to the *Ipelets* menu, and works on
  the document you are editing, usually on the objects you have
  selected.  Ipelets are good for functions that you want to use
  interactively.

Scripts and ipelets share most of what they need to know.  They use the
same classes for documents, pages, objects, and geometry, and the same
conventions.  The differences are in how they are started and how they
treat the document:

|  | Script | Ipelet |
|---|---|---|
| Started by | `ipescript` on the command line | the *Ipelets* menu (or a keyboard shortcut) in the Ipe editor |
| Document | loads and saves it itself | the document being edited, accessed through the *model* |
| Changing the document | directly | **never directly**: it registers an undo item with the model |
| User interface | command-line arguments, `print`, files | dialogs, selection, mouse position, status bar |
| Placed in | Ipe's scripts folder | Ipe's ipelets folder |

The rest of this chapter first introduces the common Lua library, then
describes scripts and ipelets in turn.  The complete reference for the
Lua library is the [Ipelib documentation](https://ipe.otfried.org/ipelib/) (look for the pages *Lua bindings
for ...*, and *Ipelets*).  The best documentation of what is possible
are the existing scripts and ipelets that come with Ipe: the scripts
are in the `scripts` folder, and the ipelets in the `ipelets`
folder of the Ipe installation (and in the Ipe source distribution).

### The Lua library in a nutshell

All of Ipe's Lua functions are in a table called `ipe`.  Here are
the most important things you need to know.

```lua
local doc = assert(ipe.Document("figure.ipe"))  -- load a document
print(#doc)                    -- number of pages
local page = doc[1]            -- pages are numbered from 1
for i, obj, selected, layer in page:objects() do
  print(i, obj:type(), layer)  -- "path", "text", "group", ...
end
local v = ipe.Vector(100, 200)
local m = ipe.Translation(v) * ipe.Rotation(math.pi / 2)
doc:save("result.ipe")
```

* Pages, views, objects, and layers are **numbered from 1**, as usual
  in Lua.  Layers are identified by their name, not by a number.

* The coordinate system is the one of the Ipe file: units are
  PostScript points (1/72 inch), the origin is at the lower left of
  the paper, and the y-axis points *up*.

* The geometric classes `ipe.Vector`, `ipe.Matrix`,
  `ipe.Line`, `ipe.Segment`, `ipe.Bezier`, and
  `ipe.Arc` are immutable values: operations create new values.
  Only `ipe.Rect` can be changed (`r:add(v)` extends the
  rectangle).  Vectors and matrices have operators:
  `v + w`, `2 * v`, `m * v`, `m1 * m2`.

* The objects you get from a page (`page[i]` or
  `page:objects()`) are the page's own objects, not copies.
  Changing such an object changes the page.  Use `obj:clone()` to
  make a copy, and `page:clone()` to make a copy of the entire
  page.

* Attributes of objects are set and read using `obj:set(name, value)` and `obj:get(name)`.  The attribute names are those
  of the Ipe editor's property boxes, for instance `stroke`,
  `fill`, `pen`, and `dashstyle`.  The value
  can be an absolute value (a number, or a color given as
  `{r=0.5, g=0.5, b=0.5}`), or a symbolic name from the stylesheet such as
  `"red"` or `"normal"`.

* Functions that read files return `nil` and an error message
  when they fail.  Calling a function with illegal arguments (such as
  a page number that does not exist) raises a Lua error.

* New objects are created with `ipe.Path`, `ipe.Text`,
  `ipe.Reference` (a symbol), `ipe.Group`, and
  `ipe.Image`.  The first three take a table with the attributes
  of the object (in an ipelet, `model.attributes` is such a
  table) and the data of the object.  A path's geometry is described by a
  *shape*, a Lua table.  For instance, a circle with radius *r* and
  center *c* is `{ { type="ellipse"; ipe.Matrix(r, 0, 0, r, c.x, c.y) } }`.  The reference documentation explains shapes in detail.

### Writing scripts

A script is a Lua file in one of Ipe's script folders.  The script
`count-objects.lua` is run by saying

```console
ipescript count-objects figure.ipe
```

(Do not write the extension `.lua`.)  The command-line arguments
are available in the global table `argv`.  Ipe looks for scripts
in the current directory, in the user's script folder
(`~/.local/share/ipe/scripts` on Linux,
`~/Library/Ipe/Scripts` on MacOS), and in the system-wide script
folder.  The environment variable `IPESCRIPTS` changes this, see
"Environment variables".

Here is a script that prints how many objects of each type there are on
every page of a document:

```lua
-- Count the objects in an Ipe document, page by page.
--
-- Usage: ipescript count-objects <document>

if #argv ~= 1 then
  io.stderr:write("Usage: ipescript count-objects <document>\n")
  return
end

local doc = assert(ipe.Document(argv[1]))

for pno, page in doc:pages() do
  -- count the objects of every type (group, text, path, image, reference)
  local counts = {}
  for _, obj, _, layer in page:objects() do
    local t = obj:type()
    counts[t] = (counts[t] or 0) + 1
  end
  local parts = {}
  for t, n in pairs(counts) do
    parts[#parts + 1] = n .. " " .. t
  end
  table.sort(parts)
  print(string.format("Page %d: %d objects (%s)", pno, #page, table.concat(parts, ", ")))
end
```

A script can do anything that Lua can do, and has the entire document
at its disposal, so it can modify it directly.  Here is a script that
makes all paths of a document red, and saves the result in a new file:

```lua
-- Make all paths in an Ipe document red.
--
-- Usage: ipescript red-paths <input> <output>
--
-- A script owns the document, so it can modify it directly.
-- Compare with ipelet-red-paths.lua, which does the same inside Ipe.

if #argv ~= 2 then
  io.stderr:write("Usage: ipescript red-paths <input> <output>\n")
  return
end

local doc = assert(ipe.Document(argv[1]))

for _, page in doc:pages() do
  for i, obj in page:objects() do
    if obj:type() == "path" then
      -- change the page (and not only the object), so that the page
      -- knows that the object's bounding box may have changed
      page:setAttribute(i, "stroke", "red")
    end
  end
end

assert(doc:save(argv[2]))
```

Here is a Lua script that reads an Ipe document and then recenters
each page on the paper.

```lua
-- recenter.lua
-- center objects on each page of the document

if #argv ~= 2 then
  io.stderr:write("Usage: ipescript recenter <inputfile> <outputfile>\n")
  return
end

inname = argv[1]
outname = argv[2]

doc = assert(ipe.Document(inname))

-- make sure we have size information for text
assert(doc:runLatex())

layout = doc:sheets():find("layout")
fs = layout.framesize

for i,p in doc:pages() do
  box = ipe.Rect()
  for j = 1,#p do
    box:add(p:bbox(j))
  end
  nx = (fs.x - box:width()) / 2
  ny = (fs.y - box:height()) / 2
  trans = ipe.Vector(nx, ny) - box:bottomLeft()
  m = ipe.Translation(trans)
  for j = 1,#p do
    p:transform(j, m)
  end
end
doc:save(outname)

```

The following script prints out all the gradients defined in a
document:

```lua
-- -*- lua -*-

function printTable(t, indent)
  for k in pairs(t) do
    local v = t[k]
    if type(v) == "table" then 
      print(indent .. k .. ":")
      printTable(v, "  " .. indent)
    else
      print(indent .. k .. ": " .. tostring(v))
    end
  end
end

if #argv ~= 1 then
  io.stderr:write("Usage: ipescript show-gradients <ipe-document>\n")
  return
end

local figname = argv[1]
local doc = assert(ipe.Document(figname))
local s = doc:sheets()

for _,w in ipairs(s:allNames("gradient")) do
  print("Gradient: ", w)
  local g = s:find("gradient", w)
  printTable(g, "  ")
end
```

Here is a script that shows how to add a gradient to a document (the
same technique works for tilings and effects). The script simply adds
to the top style sheet - in general this is not a good idea, as you
shouldn't modify the distributed style sheets (updating style sheets
from Ipe would lose the modifications), and if the document has only
the built-in style sheet, the change would not be preserved at all.

```lua
-- -*- lua -*-

if #argv ~= 1 then
  io.stderr:write("Usage: ipescript add-gradient <ipe-document>\n")
  return
end

local figname = argv[1]
local doc = assert(ipe.Document(figname))

local sheet = [[<ipestyle>
<gradient name="ball" type="radial" coords="-4 10 2 0 0 18">
 <stop offset="0" color="1 1 0"/>
 <stop offset="1" color="0 1 0"/>
</gradient>
</ipestyle>]]

local ts = ipe.Sheet(nil, sheet)

local s = doc:sheets()
for i = 1,s:count() do
  print(s:sheet(i):name())
end

-- add the gradient to the sheet on top of the stack
-- in general it is not a good idea to change the "basic" sheet,
-- better verify if a custom sheet for gradients exists already
-- and create it if not.
s:sheet(1):addFrom(ts, "gradient", "ball")
assert(doc:runLatex())
doc:save(figname .. ".new.ipe")
```

Ipe comes with several scripts that are good starting points for your
own scripts.  For instance, *onepage* collapses all pages of a document
into the layers of a single page, *scratchpad* prepares a presentation
for annotating during the talk, and *update-styles* updates the
stylesheets in many documents.

### Writing ipelets

An ipelet is a Lua file in one of Ipe's ipelet folders.  Ipe loads all
ipelets when it starts.  The ipelet folders are the system-wide folder
that comes with Ipe, and the user's own folder
(`~/.local/share/ipe/ipelets` on Linux,
`~/Library/Ipe/Ipelets` on MacOS; you can find the exact location
under *Help → Show configuration*, and change it
using the environment variable `IPELETPATH`, see "Environment variables").

An ipelet defines some global variables that tell Ipe about it:

* `label`: the name of the ipelet in the *Ipelets* menu.  A file that does not define a label is not shown in the menu (this is how you can write customizations of Ipe).

* `about`: a string shown in *Help → Ipelet information*.

* `run`: the function to call when the ipelet is invoked.

* `methods`: for an ipelet with several functions, a table with one entry for each function.  Each entry is a table with a `label` (the text of its menu entry) and optionally a `run` function (if it has none, the global `run` is called).

* `category`: optional: the submenu of the *Ipelets* menu in which the ipelet appears.  (The menu is set up by `prefs.ipelet_menu`.)

When the user invokes the ipelet, Ipe calls the `run` function with two
arguments: the **model**, which represents the document window, and the
number of the method (always 1 for an ipelet with a single function).

The simplest possible ipelet draws a circle at the mouse position:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Draw a circle at the mouse position
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- Creating a single new object is the simplest case: model:creation
-- registers the undo item for you.

label = "Circle"

about = [[
Draw a circle with radius 32 at the current mouse position.
]]

function run(model)
  local center = model.ui:pos()   -- mouse position, after snapping
  local radius = 32
  -- an ellipse is given by the matrix that maps the unit circle to it
  local shape = { { type = "ellipse";
		    ipe.Matrix(radius, 0, 0, radius, center.x, center.y) } }
  local obj = ipe.Path(model.attributes, shape)
  model:creation("create circle", obj)
end
```

Save this in your ipelet folder as `circle.lua`, restart Ipe, and
you will find *Circle* in the *Ipelets* menu.  If you set
`prefs.developer = true` in your `customization.lua` (see
"Customizing Ipe"), the *Help* menu has a *Developer* submenu with an
entry *Help → Developer → Reload ipelets*, so you do
not need to restart Ipe after every change.

Keyboard shortcuts can be assigned in `customization.lua` using the
name of the ipelet's file (without the extension) and the number of the
method, for instance `shortcuts.ipelet_1_circle = "Ctrl+Alt+C"`.

#### The ipelet's environment

Each ipelet runs in a private environment, so you do not have to worry
about polluting the global namespace.  The following names are
available inside an ipelet: `ipe`, `ipeui`, `math`,
`string`, `table`, `assert`, `ipairs`,
`pairs`, `print`, `tonumber`, `tostring`, and
the Ipe tables `prefs`, `config`, `shortcuts`, and
`mouse`.  Everything else, such as `type`, `pcall`,
`io`, `os`, or the Lua code of Ipe, must be accessed
through `_G`, for instance `_G.type(x)` or
`_G.revertOriginal`.  (Writing `type(x)` gives the error
"attempt to call a nil value (global 'type')".)

Text printed with `print` appears on the terminal from which you
started Ipe.

#### The model, and why you must not touch the document

The model is a Lua object with these members:

* `model.doc`: the document being edited.

* `model.pno`, `model.vno`: the number of the current page and view.

* `model:page()`: the current page.

* `model:selection()`: a table with the numbers of the selected objects of the current page.

* `model.attributes`: the attributes currently set in the property boxes of the user interface (a table you can pass to `ipe.Path` and friends).

* `model.snap`: the current snapping settings.

* `model.ui`: the user interface, with for instance `model.ui:pos()` (the mouse position after snapping), `model.ui:win()` (the window, to be used as the parent of dialogs), and `model.ui:explain(text)` (shows text in the status bar).

* `model:warning(text, details)`: shows a warning box.

* `model:getString(prompt, caption, initial)`: asks the user for a string (returns `nil` if the user cancels).

An ipelet has access to the live document, but it must **not modify
it directly**.  The Ipe editor keeps an undo stack, and it does not
notice if the document changes behind its back.  An ipelet that changes
the page directly breaks undo and redo, may corrupt the document, and
does not mark the document as modified.  Instead, the ipelet makes its
changes through an **undo item**.  This is a table with at least these
fields:

* `label`: a text for the status bar and the undo history (**Undo 'label'**).

* `pno`, `vno`: the page and view to show after an undo or redo.

* `undo`, `redo`: functions that are called with the undo item and the document. `redo` makes the change, `undo` reverts it.

The ipelet creates the item and passes it to `model:register(t)`, which
calls `t.redo(t, model.doc)` to perform the change, remembers the
selection, and puts the item on the undo stack.  The ipelet should
**not** change the document itself, and neither should it keep any
reference to the objects of the document: the item's `redo` and
`undo` functions are the only code that may touch the document
after the item has been registered.

There are three ways to create an undo item, from the simplest to the most
general one.

**1. Use one of the model's helper functions.**  `model:creation(label, obj)` inserts a new object on the current page (as in the circle
ipelet above), `model:transformation(label, matrix)` transforms the
selected objects, and `model:setAttribute(name, value)` sets an
attribute of the selected objects.  These functions create and
register the undo item for you.  The next ipelet uses
`model:transformation`, and also shows how to ask the user for
a value in a dialog:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Scale the selection by a factor entered by the user
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- This ipelet shows a dialog to ask for the scale factor, and then uses
-- model:transformation, which takes care of undo and redo when all you
-- want to do is to transform the selected objects by a matrix.

label = "Scale selection"

about = [[
Scale the selected objects around the center of their bounding box.
]]

function run(model)
  local selection = model:selection()  -- table with object numbers
  if #selection == 0 then
    model:warning("Nothing is selected")
    return
  end

  local d = ipeui.Dialog(model.ui:win(), "Scale selection")
  d:add("label", "label", { label = "Scale factor" }, 1, 1)
  d:add("factor", "input", { select_all = true }, 1, 2)
  d:set("factor", "2")
  d:addButton("ok", "&Ok", "accept")
  d:addButton("cancel", "&Cancel", "reject")
  if not d:execute() then return end

  local factor = tonumber(d:get("factor"))
  if not factor or factor <= 0 then
    model:warning("The scale factor must be a positive number")
    return
  end

  local page = model:page()
  local box = ipe.Rect()
  for _, i in ipairs(selection) do box:add(page:bbox(i)) end
  local center = (box:bottomLeft() + box:topRight()) * 0.5

  local m = ipe.Translation(center) * ipe.Matrix(factor, 0, 0, factor)
            * ipe.Translation(-center)
  model:transformation("scale selection", m)
end
```

**2. Work on a copy of the page.**  When the ipelet changes several
objects, the easiest approach is to make two copies of the page: the
*original*, and the *final* page in which the ipelet makes all its
changes.  The undo item then simply swaps the page in the document
between these two copies, using the functions
`_G.revertOriginal` and `_G.revertFinal`.  This is the
pattern used by most of the ipelets that come with Ipe:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Make the selected paths red
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- An ipelet must not modify the document directly.  Instead, it prepares
-- the new version of the page, and registers an undo item that switches
-- between the original and the final page.  This is the simplest way to
-- write an ipelet that changes existing objects.

label = "Red paths"

about = [[
Make the stroke color of all selected paths red.
]]

function run(model)
  local t = { label = "make paths red",
	      pno = model.pno,
	      vno = model.vno,
	      original = model:page():clone(),
	      final = model:page():clone(),
	      undo = _G.revertOriginal,
	      redo = _G.revertFinal,
	    }
  local changed = false
  for i, obj, sel, layer in t.final:objects() do
    if sel and obj:type() == "path" then
      if t.final:setAttribute(i, "stroke", "red") then changed = true end
    end
  end
  if changed then
    model:register(t)
  else
    model.ui:explain("No selected path to make red")
  end
end
```

The same pattern also works to create several objects.  Here the
ipelet collects what it needs to know about the selected objects first,
and only then inserts new objects, since inserting objects while
iterating over the page would also visit the new objects:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Mark the center of the bounding box of every selected object
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- This ipelet creates several new objects at once.  It uses the same
-- undo item as ipelet-red-paths.lua: the original page and the final page.

label = "Mark centers"

about = [[
Create a mark at the center of the bounding box of every selected object.
]]

function run(model)
  local page = model:page()
  local layer = page:active(model.vno)
  local t = { label = "mark centers",
	      pno = model.pno,
	      vno = model.vno,
	      original = page:clone(),
	      final = page:clone(),
	      undo = _G.revertOriginal,
	      redo = _G.revertFinal,
	    }

  -- Collect the centers first: inserting objects while iterating over
  -- the page would visit the new objects as well.
  local centers = {}
  for i, obj, sel in t.final:objects() do
    if sel then
      local box = t.final:bbox(i)
      centers[#centers + 1] = (box:bottomLeft() + box:topRight()) * 0.5
    end
  end

  for _, center in ipairs(centers) do
    -- model.attributes are the attributes currently set in the user interface
    local mark = ipe.Reference(model.attributes, "mark/disk(sx)", center)
    t.final:insert(nil, mark, nil, layer)
  end

  if #centers > 0 then
    model:register(t)
  end
end
```

**3. Write your own undo and redo functions.**  Copying a page is easy, but
wasteful if the ipelet only changes a small thing, such as the
properties of a layer.  Then the undo item can remember what it
needs to revert its action.  The next example also shows an ipelet
with several methods:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- An ipelet with several methods, and an undo item with explicit
-- undo and redo functions
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- Cloning the whole page is simple, but wasteful when only a small
-- thing changes.  Here the undo item remembers just what is needed to
-- go back: which layers were locked before.

label = "Lock layers"

about = [[
Lock or unlock all layers of the current page.
]]

-- The method is called with the model and the number of the method.
local function lock_layers(model, num)
  local locked = (num == 1)
  local page = model:page()
  local was_locked = {}
  for _, layer in ipairs(page:layers()) do
    was_locked[layer] = page:isLocked(layer)
  end

  local t = { label = locked and "lock all layers" or "unlock all layers",
	      pno = model.pno,
	      vno = model.vno,
	      locked = locked,
	      was_locked = was_locked,
	    }
  -- redo is also called to perform the action the first time
  t.redo = function (t, doc)
    for layer in pairs(t.was_locked) do
      doc[t.pno]:setLocked(layer, t.locked)
    end
  end
  t.undo = function (t, doc)
    for layer, was in pairs(t.was_locked) do
      doc[t.pno]:setLocked(layer, was)
    end
  end
  model:register(t)
end

methods = {
  { label = "Lock all layers", run = lock_layers },
  { label = "Unlock all layers", run = lock_layers },
}
```

If your ipelet changes the stylesheets of the document, set
`t.style_sheets_changed = true` in the undo item, so that Ipe updates the
lists of symbolic names in the user interface after an undo or redo.

#### Dialogs

Ipelets can show dialogs using `ipeui.Dialog`, as in the scale example
above.  Dialogs can contain labels, input fields, text boxes, lists,
combo boxes, check boxes, and image previews, arranged in a grid.  See the
Ipelib documentation (*Lua bindings for dialogs and menus*) for
all the details, and the ipelets *search-replace* and *selectby* that
come with Ipe for more examples.

#### Testing an ipelet without the editor

It is tedious to test an ipelet by starting the Ipe editor, loading a
document, selecting objects, and invoking the ipelet.  The script
*run-ipelet* that comes with Ipe runs an ipelet on a document from the
command line, with a model that behaves like the one in the editor
(it uses the real model of the Ipe editor, including its undo stack):

```console
ipescript run-ipelet circle.lua figure.ipe result.ipe
```

The ipelet is loaded in the same restricted environment as in the editor.
It is run with all objects of the first page selected (use the options
`--select none` or `--select 1,3` to change this, `--page`,
`--view`, and `--method` to change the page, the view, and the number of
the method to run).  The result is saved as `result.ipe`.

The script then undoes and redoes the changes made by the ipelet, using
Ipe's own undo and redo, and checks that the page is restored exactly.
This finds the most common mistake in ipelets, namely
not registering an undo item or not reverting everything in the
`undo` function:

```console
$ ipescript run-ipelet scale.lua figure.ipe result.ipe factor=3
Running scale on page 1, view 1 with 3 selected objects
[dialog] Scale selection
[dialog]   factor = 3
[explain] scale selection
1 undo item(s) registered: scale selection
[explain] Undo 'scale selection'
Undo restores the original page: OK
[explain] Redo 'scale selection'
Redo restores the result: OK
Saved result.ipe
```

Dialogs cannot be shown by this script.  Instead, a dialog behaves as if
the user had accepted it (or canceled it, if you pass `--cancel`), and
with every element having the value set by the ipelet.  You can give a
different value by adding arguments of the form *name=value*, as in the
example above, where `factor=3` sets the value of the dialog
element `factor`.  The exit status of *run-ipelet* is not zero
if the ipelet fails or the undo check finds a problem.

*run-ipelet* takes the Lua code of the Ipe editor from your Ipe
installation.  If you want to test with a different version (for
instance a source tree), set the environment variable `IPELUAPATH` to a Lua
path such as `/path/to/ipe/src/ipe/lua/?.lua`.

*run-ipelet* has no canvas and does not run LaTeX, so it cannot test
ipelets that depend on them.  It is very useful for everything else,
and also makes it possible to write automatic tests for your ipelets.

#### C++ ipelets

Ipelets can also be written in C++, which is useful if you already have
code for some geometric computation, or want to use a library such as
CGAL.  Such an ipelet consists of a shared library, and a small Lua file
that declares its label and its methods, and calls the C++ code.
The details are described in the Ipelib documentation (see the page *Ipelets*).

### Writing scripts and ipelets with an AI assistant

AI assistants (large language models) can write simple scripts and
ipelets for you.  The result will be much better if the assistant has
the right information.  For this purpose, the Ipe manual is also published
as plain text, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention:
the file [llms.txt](https://otfried.github.io/ipe/llms.txt) is an index
for assistants, and [llms-full.txt](https://otfried.github.io/ipe/llms-full.txt) contains this chapter and
the complete reference of the Lua library in a single file, which you can
give to your assistant (or paste into its instructions).  If you work with a
coding assistant in your ipelet folder, copy the file [AGENTS-ipelets.md](https://otfried.github.io/ipe/AGENTS-ipelets.md) there under the name
`AGENTS.md`: many assistants read such a file automatically.  It tells
the assistant where to find the documentation, summarizes the most important
rules, and asks it to test its ipelets with *run-ipelet*.

If you prefer to select the material yourself, we suggest to give it:

* this chapter of the manual, and the reference of the Lua library (the
  page *Lua bindings* of the Ipelib documentation, which lists all
  functions, and the page about dialogs if your ipelet has a dialog),

* one or two existing scripts or ipelets that are similar to what you
  need (the examples in this chapter, or the ones that come with Ipe).

Tell the assistant that it must write a script or an ipelet (it
matters, see above), what the objects it works on are, and
what should happen.  Then check the result carefully before using it
on a precious document.

If you use an assistant that can run commands, tell it about
*run-ipelet*: it can then test the ipelet on a sample document,
see the error messages and the result of the undo check, and fix its code
without your help.  Ipelets that modify the document without registering
an undo item are the most common problem of ipelets written without
testing.  Here is the output of *run-ipelet* for the example
`ipelet-wrong.lua`, which changes the page directly:

```lua
----------------------------------------------------------------------
-- WRONG: an ipelet that modifies the document without an undo item
----------------------------------------------------------------------
--
-- This ipelet is an example of what *not* to do.  The page is changed
-- directly, so Ipe does not know about the change: the document is not
-- marked as modified, and undo and redo no longer work correctly.
-- Run it with ipescript run-ipelet to see the warning.

label = "Wrong"

about = "Do not write ipelets like this."

function run(model)
  local page = model:page()
  for i, obj, sel in page:objects() do
    if sel and obj:type() == "path" then
      page:setAttribute(i, "stroke", "red")   -- no undo item!
    end
  end
end
```

```console
$ ipescript run-ipelet ipelet-wrong.lua figure.ipe result.ipe
Running ipelet-wrong on page 1, view 1 with 3 selected objects
The ipelet did not register an undo item.
WARNING: the page has been modified without registering an undo item!
Saved result.ipe
```

## Lua API reference

### Ipelets written in Lua

Ipelets written in Lua have access to the entire Ipe user interface,
and can in principle do anything that Ipe can do.

An ipelet is a Lua script that is placed in Ipe's ipelet directory.

The script needs to define three global variables, namely `label`, `about`, and either `run` or `methods` (or both).

* `label` is a string containing the label (that is, the name) of
  the ipelet.  It is shown in the Ipelet menu.

* `about` is a string containing an 'about' or copyright notice for
      the ipelet.  Ipe displays this in the "About the ipelets" box.

* `run` is used if the ipelet contains only a single method.
    When the ipelet is invoked, the function `run` is called by Lua.

* `methods` is used if the ipelet contains more than one method.
    It is an array with an entry for each method.  Each entry is a
    table with keys `label` (defining the label of the method) and
    `run` (a Lua function that will be called by Ipe to execute this
    method).  If an entry does not have a `run` field, then the
    global `run` method is called instead.

If an ipelet defines no `label` variable, then the ipelet is not
added to the Ipelet menu.  Such ipelets can be used to customize Ipe.

If an ipelet has a `category`, it is placed in that submenu of the
Ipelet menu (see `prefs.ipelet_menu` in *prefs.lua*).

When Ipe invokes an ipelet, the Lua method is called with two
arguments: the first argument *model* is the active Ipe user
interface (the "model" of the document window), the second is the index
of the method being invoked (always 1 if the ipelet has a single `run` function).  A keyboard shortcut for method number *n* of the ipelet in
file *name.lua* is defined by setting `shortcuts.ipelet_n_name`.

The "global" environment of the ipelet is a private environment for
this ipelet only, so there is no need to fear polluting the global
namespace - you can use names here freely.  Only the following names
have been imported from Ipe's global namespace: `_G`, `ipe`, `ipeui`, `math`, `string`, `table`, `assert`, `ipairs`, `pairs`, `print`, `tonumber`, `tostring`, `shortcuts`, `prefs`,
`config`, and `mouse`.  You can access any others you may need
through `_G` (for instance `_G.type` or `_G.revertOriginal`).

The manual (chapter "Scripts and ipelets") has a tutorial with
examples.  See also "Programming in Lua" for the bindings of the Ipe objects, and
"Lua bindings for dialogs and menus" for dialogs.

#### Undo items

It is important that the ipelet does *not* directly modify the
document.  This would mess up the undo stack, and could cause Ipe to
crash on undo or redo.  Instead, to modify the document the ipelet
needs to create an undo item `t` and call `model:register(t)`.

An undo item is a Lua table with the following fields:
```lua
t.label   -- string, shown to the user ("Undo 'label'")
t.pno     -- page number to show after undo and redo
t.vno     -- view number to show after undo and redo
t.undo    -- function t.undo(t, doc) that reverts the change
t.redo    -- function t.redo(t, doc) that makes the change

-- optional:
t.style_sheets_changed = true  -- if the style sheets of doc are changed
```
`model:register(t)` records the selection, calls `t.redo` with the item and the
document `model.doc` to make the change, and puts `t` on the undo stack.  A page-wide change
is easily implemented by making copies of the page before and after the
change, and switching between them:
```lua
local t = { label = "my change", pno = model.pno, vno = model.vno,
            original = model:page():clone(),
            final = model:page():clone(),
            undo = _G.revertOriginal,   -- doc:set(t.pno, t.original)
            redo = _G.revertFinal }     -- doc:set(t.pno, t.final)
-- modify t.final here (not model:page()!)
model:register(t)
```

#### The model

The model has the following members and methods:
```lua
model.doc          -- the document
model.pno          -- current page number
model.vno          -- current view number
model.file_name    -- name of the file, or nil
model.attributes   -- attributes currently set in user interface
                   -- (a table suitable for ipe.Path, ipe.Text, ipe.Reference)
model.snap         -- currently active snap settings (see below)
model.ui           -- the AppUi object (see \ref luaappui)

model:page()       -- returns current page
model:selection()  -- table with the numbers of the selected objects
                   -- of the current page

model:register(t)  -- register undo item and execute its redo method

-- register undo items for the most common changes:
model:creation(label, obj)       -- insert obj into the active layer;
                                 -- obj becomes the only selected object
model:transformation(label, m, deselect)
                                 -- transform selected objects by matrix m
model:setAttribute(property, value)
                                 -- set property of selected objects

model:warning(text, details)     -- display a warning box

-- ask the user for a value; return nil if the user cancels:
s = model:getString(prompt, caption, initial)  -- caption and initial are optional
n = model:getDouble(caption, label, initial, minimum, maximum)
```

Useful methods of `model.ui` are `win()` (the window to be used as the
parent of dialogs), `explain(text)` (show text in the status bar), `pos()` (mouse position, after snapping), and `zoom()`.

#### Testing ipelets

The script *run-ipelet* (run as `ipescript run-ipelet`) runs a
Lua ipelet on a document without starting the Ipe editor.  It uses the
`model` of the Ipe editor with a user interface that does nothing, runs
the ipelet, saves the result, and checks that undo and redo restore the
page exactly.  Dialogs behave as if accepted.  See the manual for details.

Look at the existing ipelets for inspiration.

// --------------------------------------------------------------------

### Programming in Lua

The library *libipelua* implements Lua bindings for many classes in
Ipelib.  The bindings are available in Lua ipelets, as well as in Lua
scripts executed using the ipescript program.

These pages document the Lua bindings to Ipelib:

* Lua bindings for geometric objects
* Lua bindings for objects and attributes
* Lua bindings for Document, Page, and StyleSheet

When writing Ipelets in Lua, you have access to additional methods
provided by the Ipe program itself:

* Lua bindings for Ipe
* Lua bindings for dialogs and menus

### Lua bindings for geometric objects

All Ipelib objects have constructors of the form:

```lua
 v = ipe.Vector()
 m = ipe.Matrix()
 m = ipe.Translation()  -- another Matrix constructor
 m = ipe.Rotation()     -- yet another Matrix constructor
 r = ipe.Rect()
 l = ipe.Line()
 l = ipe.LineThrough()  -- another Line constructor
 l = ipe.Bisector()     -- yet another Line constructor
 s = ipe.Segment()
 b = ipe.Bezier()
 a = ipe.Arc()
```

Note that ipe::Angle and ipe::Linear are not bound in Lua.  Use
numbers and ipe.Matrix instead.  A useful method for angles is:
```lua
beta = ipe.normalizeAngle(alpha, lowLimit)
```

#### Vector

*ipe.Vector* binds ipe::Vector. There are the following methods:
```lua
v = ipe.Vector()         -- zero vector
v = ipe.Vector(x, y)
v = ipe.Direction(alpha) -- unit vector in this direction 
a = v.x                  -- read only access to x and y coordinates
b = v.y

v:len() -- returns norm of vector
v:sqLen() -- returns square of norm
v:normalized() -- returns this vector normalized
v:orthogonal() -- returns this vector rotated left by 90 degrees
v:factorize(u) -- factors v = lambda u + x, where x orth. to u, u is unit
v:angle()     -- return direction 
v == w        -- vector equality
v ~= w
-v            -- unary minus
v + w         -- vector addition
v - w         -- vector difference
5 * v         -- multiplication with a scalar
v * 5         -- multiplication with a scalar
v ^ w         -- dot product
```

#### Matrix

*ipe.Matrix* binds ipe::Matrix. It has the following methods:
```lua
m = ipe.Matrix()                        -- identity matrix
m = ipe.Matrix(a1, a2, a3, a4)		-- linear transformation
m = ipe.Matrix(a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6)  -- affine transformation
m = ipe.Matrix( { a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6 } ) -- same from table
m = ipe.Rotation(alpha)                 -- rotation matrix
m = ipe.Translation(v)                  -- v is a vector
m = ipe.Translation(x, y)

m1 == m2          -- matrix equality
m1 * m2           -- matrix multiplication
m * v             -- matrix * vector
m * arc		  -- matrix * arc

m:elements()      -- returns six-element array with elements
m:coeff()         -- same as m:elements()

m:isIdentity()
m:isSingular(threshold)
m:inverse()
m:translation()   -- return translation component
m:linear()        -- returns matrix without the translation component
```

#### Rect

*ipe.Rect* binds ipe::Rect.  This is the only mutable geometric
object - take care not to be surprised when *ipe.Rect* objects are
shared. 

It has the following methods:
```lua
r = ipe.Rect()    -- empty
r:isEmpty()
r:topRight()
r:bottomLeft()
r:topLeft()
r:bottomRight()
r:left()
r:right()
r:bottom()
r:top()
r:width()
r:height()
r:add(v)          -- extend to cover vector v
r1:add(r2)        -- extend to cover rectangle r2
r1:clipTo(r2)     -- clip r1 to lie inside r2
r:contains(v)     
r1:contains(r2)
r1:intersects(r2)
```

#### Line

*ipe.Line* binds ipe::Line. It has the following methods:

```lua
l = ipe.Line(p, dir)      -- dir must be unit vector
l = ipe.LineThrough(p, q)
l = ipe.Bisector(p, q)

-- l:side() returns +1 if v lies to the left side of the line, 
-- 0 if on line, -1 if on the right side
l:side(v)                 
l:point()                 -- starting point of line
l:dir()                   -- unit direction vector
l:normal()                -- unit normal vector pointing to the left side
l:distance(v)             -- returns distance from point to line
l1:intersects(l2)         -- returns intersection point or nil
l:project(p)              -- projection of point on line
```

#### Segment

*ipe.Segment* binds ipe::Segment. It has the following methods:

```lua
s = ipe.Segment(p, q)	
p, q = s:endpoints()      -- returns both endpoints
s:line()                  -- returns an ipe.Line
s:project(p)              -- returns projection or nil
s:distance(p)
s:intersects(l)           -- return intersection point or nil
s1:intersects(s2)
```

#### Bezier

*ipe.Bezier* binds ipe::Bezier. It has the following methods:

```lua
b = ipe.Bezier(v1, v2, v3, v4)	
b = ipe.Quad(v1, v2, v3)  -- quadratic Bezier (control points v1, v2, v3),
                          -- returned as a cubic Bezier
b:point(t)                -- point at value t
v1, v2, v3, v4 = b:controlpoints()  -- returns all four control points
b:bbox()
t, p = b:snap(pos)

-- intersections: 
-- x is line, segment, or bezier
-- returns table of intersection points
b:intersect(x)
```

#### Arc

*ipe.Arc* binds ipe::Arc. It has the following methods:

```lua
a = ipe.Arc(m)            -- ellipse defined by ipe.Matrix m
a = ipe.Arc(m, p, q)      -- arc from p to q
a = ipe.Arc(m, alpha, beta)

a:endpoints()             -- returns two endpoints
a:angles()                -- returns two angles
a:bbox()
a:matrix()
a:isEllipse() 
alpha, p = a:snap(pos)

-- intersections: 
-- x is line, segment, arc, or bezier
-- returns table of intersection points
a:intersect(x)
```

### Lua bindings for objects and attributes

The five Ipe objects are ipe::Group, ipe::Path, ipe::Text, ipe::Image,
and ipe::Reference.  They can be constructed from Lua as follows:

```lua
obj = ipe.Reference(attributes, name, pos)
obj = ipe.Text(attributes, text, pos)          -- Text of type label
obj = ipe.Text(attributes, text, pos, width)   -- Text of type minipage
obj = ipe.Path(attributes, shape, with_arrows)	 
obj = ipe.Group(elements)       -- elements is a table of objects
obj = ipe.Image(rect, bitmap)   -- where bitmap is another Image object 
obj = ipe.Image(rect, path)     -- to create an external image
obj = ipe.Object(xml)           -- parse an object from its XML representation
```

Here, `attributes` is a table defining the desired attributes, see
below.  `shape` is a table defining a shape, see below.  To create
path with arrows, you need to set `with_arrows` to true (it defaults
to false). The arrow settings are then used from the `attributes`.

`ipe.Object` parses the XML representation of a single object (as
returned by `obj:xml())`, and returns nil if parsing fails.  If the
string is an `<ipeselection>` (as used for the clipboard), it
instead returns two tables, with the objects and with the names of
their layers.

A bitmap can be created by reading from an image file:
```lua
bitmap, res = ipe.readImage(fname)
```
If reading the bitmap fails, then bitmap is nil and res is an error
message. Otherwise, bitmap is an Image object and res is the
resolution in dots per inch.  This will be (0,0) if the file does not
contain that information.

Objects have the following methods:
```lua
obj:type()    -- return type as string: group, text, path, image, reference
obj:clone()   -- clone the object

obj:set(property, value)    -- see below
obj:get(property)           -- see below

obj:xml()                   -- return XML representation
obj:matrix()
obj:setMatrix(m)
obj:addToBBox(r, m)         -- including control points
obj:addToBBox(r, m, false)  -- without control points

obj:setAnimate(s)           -- set string s as animate name
s = obj:getAnimate()

obj:setCustom(s)            -- set string s as custom field
s = obj:getCustom()

-- text and reference objects only:
v = obj:position()
-- reference objects only:
name = obj:symbol()          -- the name of the symbol
-- text objects only:
obj:setText(str)
str = obj:text()
width, height, depth = obj:dimensions()
-- path objects only:
shape = obj:shape()                      
obj:setShape(shape)            
-- group objects only:
n = obj:count()                  
shape = obj:clip()           -- nil if no clipping
obj:setClip(shape)
str = obj:text()             -- the link action (URL)
obj:setText(str)
-- image objects only:
rect = obj:rect()            -- image rectangle before applying obj:matrix()
obj:info()                   -- returns table about bitmap
obj:setPath(path)            -- set the path of an external image
-- write the bitmap to a file, as PNG or JPEG (without re-encoding),
-- returns true if successful:
ok = obj:saveImage(filename)
-- write raw pixel data to a file (for debugging): a PyRGBA header
-- followed by RGBA bytes, or the JPEG data for a JPEG image
obj:savePixels(filename)
obj:setBitmap(image)         -- copies image's internal bitmap and clears the external path;
                            -- preserves the rectangle and all attributes; rejects images without a bitmap
-- group objects only:
elements = obj:elements()    -- returns table with clones of elements 
element = obj:element(i)     -- returns clone of element #i
obj:elementType(i)           -- returns type of element #i
obj:replace(i, element)      -- replaces element #i with a clone; other copies of the group are unchanged
```

#### Attributes

Attributes are represented in Lua as follows:

* Symbolic names are strings

* Absolute string values (e.g. dash style) are strings

* Absolute numeric values are numbers

* Absolute colors are tables with three entries with keys `r`, `g`, `b`

* Boolean values (for `minipage`, `farrow`, `rarrow`) are
    booleans (but the strings "true" and "false" can be used to set them)

* Transformations, Pinned, Linejoin, Linecap, Fillrule, Horizontal
alignment, and Vertical alignment are represented by fixed strings,
see table below.  

The *attributes* argument to the object constructors is a table
defining all desired attributes.  Keys in the table are as follows. 
If a key is not present, the default value is used.
```lua
pathmode -- "stroked", "strokedfilled", "filled"
stroke   -- symbolic or color
fill     -- symbolic or color
dashstyle -- symbolic or absolute string
pen      -- symbolic or number
farrow   -- boolean
rarrow   -- boolean
farrowshape -- symbolic
rarrowshape -- symbolic
arrowsize  -- symbolic or number
symbolsize -- symbolic or number
symbolshape -- symbolic
textsize   -- symbolic or number
transformabletext -- boolean
textstyle  -- symbolic
opacity    -- symbolic
tiling     -- symbolic
decoration -- symbolic ("normal" means no decoration)
minipage   -- boolean	   
width 	   -- number
horizontalalignment -- "left", "right", "hcenter"
verticalalignment   -- "bottom", "baseline", "top", "vcenter"
linejoin            -- "normal", "miter", "round", "bevel"
linecap             -- "normal", "butt", "round", "square"
fillrule            -- "normal", "wind", "evenodd"
pinned              -- "none", "horizontal", "vertical", "fixed"
transformations     -- "translations", "rigid", "affine"
variant     -- symbolic, or "undefined"
externalimages -- boolean
```

#### Properties

The *set()* and *get()* methods allow to access the attributes of
objects.  The property names are 
```lua
    pen, symbolsize, 
    farrow, rarrow, farrowsize, rarrowsize, farrowshape, rarrowshape, 
    stroke, fill, markshape,
    pathmode, dashstyle, 
    textsize, textstyle, minipage, width, 
    opacity, tiling, gradient, 
    horizontalalignment, verticalalignment,
    linejoin, linecap, fillrule, 
    pinned, transformations,
    decoration,
    variant
```

It is okay to set a property on objects that do not support them (for
instance, "textsize" on a path object).  Reading such properties
results in an "undefined" return value.

#### Shape

The geometry of a path object and the clipping path of a group object
is an ipe::Shape.  This is represented in Lua as a pure Lua object,
namely an array with one entry per subpath.  

Each subpath is again a table with a `type` field whose value must be
one of "ellipse", "closedspline", or "curve".  

For an ellipse, element 1 of the table is the matrix.  

For a closed spline, the table contains the control points.  

For a curve, the table has a second field `closed`, which is either
`true` or `false`.  The table also has an entry for each segment of
the curve.  Each segment is again a table with a `type` field, whose
value is one of "arc", "segment", "spline", "oldspline", "cardinal",
or "spiro".  The segment table contains the control points of the
segment.  For arc segments, there is an additional `arc` field in the
segment table that contains the arc as an ipe.Arc object.  For
cardinal spline segments, there is an additional `tension` field in
the segment table.

### Lua bindings for Document, Page, and StyleSheet

#### Stylesheet

A stylesheet can be constructed by reading from a file (in XML
format), or by creating an empty stylesheet:
```lua
-- create from file:
-- returns sheet or nil, error message
sheet = ipe.Sheet("filename")
-- create from XML data:
-- returns sheet or nil, error message
sheet = ipe.Sheet(nil, "<ipestyle> ... </ipestyle>")
-- create empty stylesheet:
sheet = ipe.Sheet()    
```

Stylesheets have the following methods:
```lua
sheet:clone()            -- returns a private copy of the stylesheet
sheet:xml(with_bitmaps)  -- return XML representation 
sheet:add(kind, symbolic, value)
sheet:addFrom(other_sheet, kind, symbolic)
sheet:remove(kind, symbolic)
sheet:allNames(kind)
sheet:find(kind, name)
sheet:setAttribute(kind, name, absolute)
sheet:set(kind, value)  -- only for preamble, linejoin, linecap, fillrule
sheet:isStandard()      -- is this the built-in stylesheet?
sheet:name()            -- name of the stylesheet
sheet:setName(name)
```

`sheet:add` adds a definition for symbolic name to the stylesheet.
Permissible values for `kind` are:
```lua
 pen, symbolsize, arrowsize, color, dashstyle, textsize, textstretch, 
 textstyle, gridsize, anglesize, opacity, symbol, 
```

`sheet:addFrom` copies a definition for a gradient, tiling, or effect
from another stylesheet.  This makes it possible to create such
definitions by creating a temporary stylesheet from an XML string.

`sheet:remove` removes the definition of a symbolic name from the
stylesheet. This also works for symbols, gradients, tilings, and
effects. It is permissible to remove a symbolic name that is not
defined in the stylesheet.

`sheet:set` sets a value. Permissible values for `kind` are:
```lua
 preamble, linecap, linejoin, fillrule
```

#### Stylesheet cascade

Documents own an entire stack of style sheets, the style sheet *cascade*.  An empty style sheet cascade can be created like this:
```lua
sheets = ipe.Sheets()
```
or you can obtain one from an Ipe document.

Style sheet cascades have the following methods:
```lua
sheets1 = sheets:clone()              -- make a private copy
sheets:allNames(kind)
sheets:find(kind, symbolic)
sheets:has(kind, symbolic)
sheets:count()                        -- return number of sheets
sheets:sheet(index)                   -- return sheet at index
sheets:insert(index, style_sheet)     -- insert sheet at index
sheets:remove(index)                  -- delete a sheet
log = sheets:update(directory)        -- update style sheets from directory
```

`sheets:allNames` returns a table with all symbolic names defined in
the entire stylesheet cascade.  Permissible values for `kind` are:
```lua
 pen, symbolsize, arrowsize, color, dashstyle, textsize, textstretch, 
 textstyle, gridsize, anglesize, opacity, tiling, symbol, gradient, effect
```

`sheet:has` checks whether a symbolic name is defined in
the cascade.  Permissible values for `kind` are as for `allNames`.

`sheet:find` looks up a symbolic definition.  Permissible values for
`kind` are:
```lua
 pen, symbolsize, arrowsize, color, dashstyle, textsize, textstretch, 
 textstyle, gridsize, anglesize, opacity, symbol, 
 preamble, linecap, linejoin, fillrule, layout
```

#### Page

Page objects can be created like this:
```lua
p = ipe.Page()   -- create basic page with one layer and one view
p1 = p:clone()   -- returns a copy of the page
```

The following methods get and set the page style. The style name must be
defined by a `<pagestyle>` element in a style sheet. Passing `nil` to
`setStyle` clears the page style.
```lua
name = p:style()       -- return the page style name
p:setStyle(name)       -- use "normal" to reset
```

The following methods act on the **views** of a page.  Note that views
are indexed starting from 1, as usual in Lua.
```lua
p:countViews() 
p:effect(view)
p:setEffect(view, effect)
p:active(view)
p:setActive(view, layer)
p:insertView(view, layer)
p:removeView(view)
p:clearViews()
f = p:markedView(view) -- return true/false
p:setMarkedView(view, f)
name = p:viewName(view)
p:setViewName(view, name)
map = p:viewMap(view)
p:setViewMap(view, map)
lm = p:layerMatrices(view)
p:setLayerMatrices(view, lm)
```

The following methods act on the **layers** of a page. Note that layers
are always accessed by name, not by index as in C++.
```lua
p:countLayers()
p:layers()        -- return table of layer names
p:isLocked(layer)
p:setLocked(layer, boolean)
p:layerData(layer)    -- free-use text for that layer
p:setLayerData(layer, data)
mode = p:snapping(layer)  -- "never", "visible", or "always"
p:setSnapping(layer, mode)
p:renameLayer(oldname, newname)
-- if layer is nil, automatically create name for new layer:
p:addLayer(layer)     -- add layer at the end, return name of new layer
p:removeLayer(layer)
p:reorderLayers(order) -- order is a table with layer names
p:moveLayer(layer, target_index)
p:visible(view, layer)   -- is layer visible in view?
p:setVisible(view, layer, boolean)
```

The **objects** of a page can be accessed by indexing, using an
iterator, or with various methods. Note that object indices start with
1, as usual in Lua.
```lua
-- objects:

#p      -- return number of objects on page
p[i]    -- return object #i, where 1 <= i <= #p

-- iterate over objects of page:
for i, obj, sel, layer in p:objects() do
  print(i, obj, sel, layer)
end

p:select(objno)              -- returns nil, 1, or 2
p:setSelect(objno, status)   -- status is nil, 1, or 2
p:layerOf(objno)
p:setLayerOf(objno, layer)
p:visible(view, objno)       -- is object visible in view?
p:bbox(objno)                -- cached by page
p:invalidateBBox(objno)      -- invalidate cached bbox
p:insert(objno, object, select, layer)  -- objno == nil means append
p:remove(objno)
p:replace(objno, object)     -- automatically clones object
p:transform(objno, matrix)

-- returns distance from pos if it is less than bound
p:distance(objno, pos, bound)

-- returns true if attribute was actually changed
p:setAttribute(objno, property, value)
```

Finally, there are various methods to query and modify the currently
selected objects, the page title and sections, etc.:
```lua
-- selection:
obj = p:primarySelection() -- nil if no primary selection
p:hasSelection()           -- true or false
p:deselectAll()
p:ensurePrimarySelection()

-- variant is optional (a variant name), and defaults to no variant
title, skipped = p:title(variant)    -- skipped: is page skipped in this variant?
p:setTitle(variant, title, skipped)  -- use variant == nil for no variant

-- t is a table with fields "section" and "subsection"
-- if section or subsection is not a string, the title is used
t = p:sections()
p:setSections(t)

-- n is a string
n = p:notes()
p:setNotes(n)

-- f is true/false
f = p:marked()
p:setMarked(f)

-- XML representation, what is "ipepage" or "ipeselection" (only the
-- selected objects)
xml = p:xml(what)

-- find an edge of the page's objects near pos in the view, for snapping
-- returns origin (a vector) and direction (an angle), or nothing
origin, dir = p:findEdge(view, pos)
```

#### Document

Documents have the following methods:
```lua
doc = ipe.Document()         -- empty document
doc = ipe.Document(filename) -- load from file
doc = ipe.Document(filename, true) -- load from file, ignoring too recent Ipe version
-- returns either document or nil, error message, error code

#doc    -- number of pages
doc[i]  -- return page #i, where 1 <= i <= #doc

copy = doc:clone() -- independent pages, stylesheets, and properties;
                   -- PDF resources are not copied: run LaTeX before saving as PDF

-- format == nil: guess from filename
-- flags is either nil, or a table with keys
-- "export", "nozip", "lastview", "nocolor"
-- if format == "xml", imageFolder can be omitted
doc:save(filename, format, flags, imageFolder)  
doc:exportPages(filename, flags, fromPage, toPage, imageFolder)
doc:exportView(filename, format, flags, pageNo, viewNo, imageFolder)

-- iterating over pages of document:
for i, p in doc:pages() do
  print("Page number",  i, p)
end

doc:set(no, page)         -- replace with a clone of page, returns old page
doc:insert(no, page)
doc:append(page)
doc:remove(no)            -- returns page and removes from document
doc:countTotalViews()
doc:sheets()              -- returns style sheet cascade
old = doc:replaceSheets(sheets)  -- replace and return old cascade
doc:has(what)  -- where what in { "truetype", "gradients", "tilings", "transparency" }
doc:runLatex(docname)  -- pass filename of Ipe document or nil
-- returns either true, nil, result code, logfile
--         or     false, error message, result code, logfile

-- Running Latex in the background, as done by doc:runLatex:
-- success is true or false; if false, errmsg and errcode describe the error;
-- converter is an opaque object to be passed to completeLatexRun
-- (errcode "notext" with success true means there is no text to convert)
success, converter, errmsg, errcode = doc:prepareLatexRun()
-- returns the command line to run (a string), or nil
command = doc:howToRunLatex(docname)  -- pass filename of Ipe document or nil
-- after running the command, load the result:
-- returns success, errmsg, errcode, logfile
success, errmsg, errcode, log = doc:completeLatexRun(converter)

doc:fontPool()    -- returns light userdata
doc:checkStyle()  -- returns list of undefined symbolic names
t = doc:properties()  -- returns table
doc:setProperties(t)  -- changes properties set in table
```

`doc:properties()` returns a table with the following fields (all
fields exist even if their contents is an empty string):
```lua
title author subject keywords language preamble created modified creator
fullscreen cropbox numberpages sequentialtext tex
```

#### Other functions

```lua
ipe.fileFormat(filename)      -- returns one of "xml", "pdf", "eps", "ipe5", "unknown"
ipe.fileExists(filename)      -- returns true or false
ipe.realPath(filename)        -- convert relative path to absolute path
ipe.directory(path)           -- return table of files in directory
ipe.openFile(path, mode)      -- replacement for io.open handling Unicode on Windows
ipe.mkdir(path)               -- create directory; returns true, or nil, error message, error code
beziers = ipe.splineToBeziers(spline, is_closed, old_style)
ipelet = ipe.Ipelet(dllname)  -- loads C++ ipelet from absolute path
-- returns ipelet or nil, error message
-- run function number 'num' (starting from 1) of the ipelet;
-- returns true if the document was modified (so undo information is needed)
-- layer is the name of a layer, attributes and snap are the tables
-- described for the user interface, and helper is a table of methods
-- (message, messageBox, getString, and a table parameters) that implement the ipelet's user interface
ok = ipelet:run(num, page, doc, pageno, viewno, layer, attributes, snap, helper)

-- return the path of an Ipe folder, followed by the optional file name:
-- name is one of "lua", "icons", "doc", "styles", "ipelets", "scripts",
-- "user-styles", "user-ipelets", "user-scripts", "config", "latex"
-- (the "latex" folder is created if it does not exist)
path = ipe.folder(name)
path = ipe.folder(name, filename)
```

### Lua bindings for Ipe

These are the Lua methods provided by the Ipe program itself.  They
are only available to Lua code running inside Ipe.

#### Application user interface

The application user interface object provides the GUI for the Ipe
program. 

```lua
-- model is a Lua table containing methods that will be called 
-- by the ui when events occur
ui = AppUi(model)

-- returns window id of window
-- (to be used as parent for dialogs)
id = ui:win()

ui:close()         -- close window

ui:setActionState(name, t) -- set whether action is checked 
t = ui:actionState(name)   -- is action checked?
-- return info about action: id, and whether it's always on 
id, alwaysOn = actionInfo(name)       

ui:explain(text)     -- show message in status bar for a few seconds
ui:setWindowTitle(caption)

-- make a tool visible or invisible
-- tool is one of "layers", "properties", "bookmarks", "notes"
-- t is true or false
ui:showTool(tool, t)

ui:setNotes(n)       -- set string for Notes tool

-- set the list of recent files in the file menu (table of file names)
ui:setRecentFiles(files)

-- put the window in a screen mode: "normal", "maximized", or "full"
ui:setScreen(mode)

-- set the text of the snap indicator in the status bar
ui:setSnapIndicator(text)

-- set grid size and angle size selectors; both are numbers or symbolic names
ui:setGridAngleSize(gridsize, anglesize)

-- set the order in which symbolic names of this kind are shown in the
-- selectors (kind as for stylesheets, names is a table of strings)
ui:setPreferredOrder(kind, names)

-- return the Windows menu id of an action and whether the action is
-- always enabled (only used on Windows, to compute keyboard shortcuts)
id, alwaysOn = ui:actionInfo(name)

-- set contents of attribute selectors from style sheet
ui:setupSymbolicNames(styleSheet)

-- set attribute values displayed in user interface
-- 'attributes' table see below
ui:setAttributes(styleSheet, attributes)

-- set layer list from page
ui:setLayers(page, view)  

ui:setNumbers(?)
ui:setBookmarks(?)

-- page/view selector tool:
-- select one page and return page number (or nil if canceled)
pno = ui:selectPage(doc) 
-- select one view and return view number (or nil if canceled)
vno = ui:selectPage(doc, page_no)

ui:pageSorter(?)

ui:setClipboard(text)     -- store text on system clipboard

-- get text or image from system clipboard
-- if allowBitmap is false, only text is retrieved
-- returns:
-- "text", string  if clipboard contains text
-- "path", string  if clipboard contains name of an image file
-- "image", bitmap if clipboard contains actual pixel data
format, value = ui:getClipboard(allowBitmap)  
```

On GTK and in the JS version, the method is called `getClipboardAsync`
and delivers its result to the coroutine passed as an additional
argument.  Use `model:clipboard` instead, which hides this difference.

The following methods work on the canvas inside the UI:

```lua
ui:setPage(page, pgno, view, styleSheet) -- set page shown on canvas
ui:setSnap(snap)                    -- for 'snap' table see below
ui:setFontPool(p)       -- an opaque object obtained from an ipe.Document

-- 'pan' is a vector indicating the user coordinates at canvas center
v = ui:pan()       
ui:setPan(v)

zoom = ui:zoom()        -- a number
ui:setZoom(zoom)

v = ui:pos()            -- current mouse position, after snapping
v = ui:unsnappedPos()   -- current mouse position, before snapping
v = ui:simpleSnapPos()  -- same, but ignoring angular snap
v = ui:globalPos()      -- mouse position on screen

v, dpi = ui:canvasSize()  -- size of canvas in pixels, monitor resolution

ui:setNumbering(t)      -- true or false
ui:setFifiVisible(t)    -- true or false
ui:setInkMode(t)        -- true or false: mouse/pen input is freehand drawing

-- the canvas looks for external images relative to this folder
ui:setImageFolder(folder)
-- use the PDF resources (fonts) of this document for rendering text
ui:setResources(doc)
-- has the canvas encountered a Type 3 font since the last call?
-- (the flag is reset by this call)
t = ui:type3Font()
-- enable automatic angular snapping with this origin (a vector)
ui:setAutoOrigin(v)
ui:setSelectionVisible(t) -- true or false
ui:setPretty(t)         -- true or false

ui:setVisibleVariant(variant) -- which variant is shown in the canvas

-- setCursor only implemented on Qt.
-- Windows 8 switches to a dot cursor automatically when using the pen.
ui:setCursor(name)         -- name in "standard", "hand", "cross"
ui:setCursor(width, color) -- sets a colored dot cursor (on Qt)

ui:update()             -- update canvas and tool
ui:update(false)        -- update tool only
ui:finishTool()

ui:panTool()
ui:selectTool()
ui:transformTool()
ui:shapeTool()

-- tool for pasting an object (usually a group): obj is an object,
-- tool is a Lua tool table, which gets the additional methods
-- tool.setColor(r, g, b) and tool.setMatrix(m)
ui:pasteTool(obj, tool)
```

##### Rendering pages

A view of a page can be rendered to a file or, for PNG, into a bitmap
in memory.  The document does not need to be the one shown in the UI.

```lua
-- format is one of "svg", "png", "eps", "pdf"
-- dest is the name of the output file, or nil (only for "png")
-- zoom is the number of pixels per point (only used for "png")
-- transparent: if true, the background of a PNG is transparent
--   instead of white (only used for "png")
-- nocrop: if true, the whole paper is rendered, including background
--   and title, instead of the bounding box of the page
result = ui:renderPage(doc, pageno, viewno, format, dest, zoom,
                       transparent, nocrop)
```

If *dest* is a file name, the result is true if the file was
written, and false otherwise.

If *dest* is nil, *format* must be "png", and the result is nil if
the page is empty or the bitmap would be too large, and otherwise a
table with the fields
```lua
width=number     (number of pixel columns)
height=number    (number of pixel rows)
pixels=string    (RGBA values in row order, 4 * width * height bytes,
                  alpha is not premultiplied)
```
This is exactly the format of the *bitmap* field of an *image*
element in an ipeui dialog.  For example:
```lua
local bitmap = ui:renderPage(doc, 1, 1, "png", nil, 2.0, true, false)
d:set("preview", { bitmap=bitmap, zoom=2.0 })
```

##### Presentations

These methods create files for the HTML presentation (reveal.js), and partially
for export to PPTX (the json file will then be read by JS code that creates the
final PPTX presentation).

Page and view numbers start from 1.  Both methods return true if the file
was written.

```lua
-- write a presentation of pages from_page to to_page, based on an HTML template
ok = ui:createPresentation(doc, filename, html_template, from_page, to_page)

-- write the JSON description of the document's views;
-- if only_marked is true, only marked views are included
ok = ui:createJson(doc, filename, only_marked)
```

##### Calling JavaScript

In the JS version of Ipe (running in a browser or as  a VS Code extension), Lua code
can call methods of the JavaScript user interface object.  Note that this
is a function, not a method.  Intended for internal use.
```lua
ui.js(method, arg1, ...)   -- at most four arguments
```

##### Wait dialog

This dialog is for running an external program (that is, latex or a
text editor).  The dialog is modal, so that the program refreshes but
otherwise waits for the running command.

```lua
ui:waitDialog(command, text)
```

Here, 'command' is a string that is passed to a shell to run the
command.  The argument 'text' appears in the dialog.

The behaviour is different on differen platforms:

1. On Win32 and MacOS, the dialog has its own event loop.  A thread is
started for the command, and when the command terminates, the dialog
is closed and the function returns with the value 'true'.

2. On Qt, the dialog is modal, but lives on the main event loop. A
thread is started for the command.  If this thread terminates quickly
(e.g. around 300ms), then the function immediately returns with value
'true'.  Otherwise, the dialog appears, and the function immediately
returns with value 'false'.  In this case, the calling Lua code should
yield to return to the main event loop.  When the thread terminates,
it will resume the Lua coroutine.

3. On JS, the dialog is modal on the normal browser event loop.
'command' must be the name of a tex engine.  The method now calls the
'runLatex' method on the JS 'window' object with the command as an
argument.  This method is supposed to be an async JS function that
returns with a promise.  The 'waitDialog' method immediately returns
with value 'false'.  The JS code that hosts the Ipe WASM libraries
must ensure that when the promise is fulfilled, the 'resume' method in
the JS bindings of the 'ui' is called.  No additional threads are
started by Ipelib.

### Lua bindings for dialogs and menus

The ipeui module provides dialogs and popup menus for Lua.  It does
not depend on any other Ipe component, and can be reused in other Lua
projects.

#### Global methods

There are a few global methods in the ipeui module:
```lua
ipeui.startBrowser(url)   -- on Win32 and Cocoa only
dt = ipeui.currentDateTime() -- returns string with current date and time
```

#### Predefined dialogs

The following are predefined dialogs.  In all cases, `parent` can
either be `nil` or a Window ID.

##### File dialog

Ask the user to select a filename for opening or for saving.  'type'
is "open" or "save".  'filter' is a table with the file name
filters. Each filter has two entries in the table, one with the name
of the filter and the extensions in parenthesis (this is used by Qt),
one with the pure patterns separated by semicolons (this is also used
by Windows). Here is an example:
```lua
filter_save = { "XML (*.ipe *.xml)", "*.ipe;*.xml",
	      	"PDF (*.pdf)", "*.pdf" }
```
'dir' is the initially selected directory, or nil.  

'name' is an initial name (without path) to show as the filename, or
nil.

'selected' is the number of the initally selected file name
filter (where 1 is the first filter), or nil.

The funtion returns nil, or both a file name and the number of the
selected filter.
```lua
ipeui.fileDialog(parent, type, caption, filter, dir, name, selected)
```

##### Color dialog

```lua
-- choose a color
-- r,g,b are in the range 0.0 to 1.0
-- returns nil or a (r,g,b) triple
ipeui.getColor(parent, title, r, g, b)
```

##### Message box

```lua
-- show a message box
-- type is one of "none" "warning" "information" "question" "critical"
-- details may be nil
-- buttons may be nil (for "ok") or one of 
-- "ok" "okcancel" "yesnocancel", "discardcancel", "savediscardcancel", 
-- return 1 for ok/yes/save, 0 for no/discard, -1 for cancel
ipeui.messageBox(parent, type, text, details, buttons)
```

#### Dialogs

Other dialogs can be constructed programmatically.  A dialog consists
of various elements layed out in a grid, and a row of buttons
underneath.    Create the dialog by adding elements using 'add', and
filling the button row using 'addButton'.  The 'action' for
'addButton' can be one of the strings "accept" or "reject", or a Lua
method.
```lua
d = ipeui.Dialog(parent, window_title, language)

-- row == -1 means last row, row == 0 means start new row
d:add(name, what, options, row, column, row_span, column_span)
d:addButton(name, caption, action)

d:setStretch("row", row_number, stretch_factor)
d:setStretch("column", column_number, stretch_factor)

d:set(name, value)
value = d:get(name)

-- enable/disable elements
d:setEnabled(name, true_or_false)

-- set to ignore escape when the value of field is equal to originalValue
d:set("ignore-escape", field, originalValue)

-- show dialog modally
accepted = d:execute()
accepted = d:execute(size)   -- where size == { width, height }

-- close the dialog from a Lua method (such as the action of a button
-- or checkbox); d:execute() then returns accepted
d:accept(accepted)           -- true or false
```

Note that on some platforms (Qt and JS), `d:execute` may yield.
Closing the dialog causes the Lua thread to be resumed.

*name* can be an arbitrary string. *what* must be one of 
```lua
button, text, list, label, combo, checkbox, input, image
```
*options* is a table.  Most fields are optional:
```lua
-- button:
label="string"  (Required!)
action="accept" or "reject" or a Lua method

-- label:
label="string"  (Required!)

-- text:
read_only=bool
syntax="logfile" or "xml" or "latex"
select_all=bool
spell_check=bool
language=str

-- list and combo:
array of list items (strings)
can also contain a Lua method with key "action" (called when an item
is activated).

-- checkbox:
label="string"  (Required!)
action= Lua method  (called when state changed)

-- input:

-- image:
value=table     (see below, default is an empty preview)
width=number    (preview area width in pixels, default 180)
height=number   (preview area height in pixels, default 80)
```

An *image* element shows a preview of a bitmap inside a fixed-size
area.  It does not load or display an actual ipe::Image object.
Its *value* is a table that has exactly one of the following fields:
```lua
text="string"     (a text message)
path="string"     (the name of a PNG or JPEG file)
bitmap=table      (a bitmap in memory)
```
and optionally
```lua
zoom=number       (default 1.0)
```
A bitmap file or bitmap in memory is displayed centered in the preview
area, with each of its pixels divided by *zoom*, and scaled down to
fit the preview area if necessary.  Transparent parts show the
background of the preview area.  The *bitmap* table has the fields
```lua
width=number      (number of pixel columns)
height=number     (number of pixel rows)
pixels="string"   (RGBA values in row order, 4 * width * height bytes,
                   alpha is not premultiplied)
```
If the file cannot be loaded, or if the table is empty, a message
"Preview unavailable" is shown instead.  The *value* of an *image*
element can be changed using *set*, using a table in the same format.
Examples:
```lua
d:add("preview", "image", { width=100, height=100,
                            value={ text="No preview yet" } }, 1, 1)
d:set("preview", { path="/tmp/picture.png", zoom=2.0 })
d:set("preview", { bitmap={ width=2, height=1, pixels="\255\0\0\255\0\0\255\128" } })
```

The Lua method for button, checkbox, combo, and list is called with
the dialog as an argument.  Do not capture the dialog inside the
method, as this would create a cyclic reference that would stop the
dialog from being garbage collected! (It also causes a crash on Qt
if the dialog is destroyed by Lua after the parent window has already
deleted it.)

The argument of *set* is:
* a string value for *label*, *text*, and *input*,
* a table for *image*,
* either an integer, a string, or an array of string items for *list* and *combo*,
* a boolean for *checkbox*.

The result value of *get* is:
* a string for *text* and *input*,
* an integer for *list* (or nil if there is no current item) and *combo*,
* a boolean for *checkbox*.

#### Popup menus

Popup menus are constructed and shown as follows:
```lua
m = ipeui.Menu(parent)	
item, subitem = m:execute(global_position)
```
When the menu is cancelled, *execute* returns *nil*.

You can then add items to the menu one by one.  A simple item is added
like this:
```lua
m:add("name", "Label")
```
When this item is selected, execute returns *name*, and an empty string.

The following line adds an entire submenu:
```lua
m:add("name", "Submenu", { "alpha", "beta", "gamma" } )
```
When an item from this submenu is selected, *execute* returns *name* and the name of the submenu item.

When the strings in the table are not directly the visible labels for
the submenu, a Lua function can be used to convert them:
```lua
m:add("name", "Submenu", { "alpha", "beta", "gamma" },
      function (i, item) return "select " .. item end )
```

The final argument can either be a string or a function.
If it is a string, then all items are checkable, and the item whose
name is identical to the final argument is checked.
Otherwise, the function maps item number and
name to a color (three numbers in the range 0.0 to 1.0).  This is then
used to display a color icon. 

#### Timers

Timers are constructed as follows:
```lua
t = ipeui.Timer(table, "method")
```
When the timer times out, it will call the method named *method* in
the Lua table *table*.  The timer stores only a weak reference to the
table, so the timer will not stop the table from being garbage
collected.

The timer is controlled using the methods:
```lua
timer:setInterval(interval)     -- an integer in milliseconds
timer:setSingleShot(bool)       -- default is repeating timer
timer:start()	
timer:stop()
a = timer:active()              -- true if the timer is running
```
